title: Two-stage group testing with arithmetic progressions
formal:
Do there exist absolute constants \(C,D>0\) such that, for every pair of integers \(n\ge2\) and \(1\le k\le n\), an unknown set \(S\subseteq[n]\) with \(|S|\le k\) can be identified exactly by the following deterministic two-stage scheme?

The first stage uses at most \(Ck\log_2 n\) tests. Each test asks whether \(S\) meets a finite arithmetic progression contained in \([n]\), and every first-stage test is fixed before any answers are received. After seeing all first-stage answers, the second stage chooses at most \(Dk\) individual indices and learns their membership in \(S\). All second-stage indices must be chosen before receiving any second-stage answer. The final output must equal \(S\) for every admissible hidden set.

The constants must work simultaneously for all \(n,k,S\). The resource being bounded is the number of tests in each stage; neither constructing the scheme nor decoding the answers is subject to a running-time bound.
why: This question tests how much measurement restrictions can cost in sparse identification even when one follow-up round is available. A resolution would distinguish what arbitrary pooling achieves from what regularly spaced queries can support, a distinction motivated by pattern matching rather than by a new statistical noise model.

progress.text: De Bonis, Gąsieniec and Vaccaro give an order-optimal two-stage algorithm with unrestricted pools. This is the baseline cited by Porat; it does not impose arithmetic progressions.
Problem 33 records the progression-restricted \(O(k\log^2 n)\) bound and asks for \(O(k\log n)\), retaining only \(O(k)\) individual queries after the first-stage results.

The original problem page still presents the question, with a last edit dated March 2013. A bounded search for subsequent arithmetic-progression group-testing results found no matching resolution; the age of this page limits the current-status evidence.

category_assignment.reason: The recovered target is a restricted two-stage group-query identification algorithm.

importance.reason: A concrete query-design question connecting structured pools, sparse identification and limited adaptivity. Its contribution is narrower than unrestricted group testing, but the arithmetic-progression restriction captures a meaningful loss of query freedom and the source identifies a pattern-matching motivation.

sentences: A hidden set of at most k positions must be identified by noiseless yes/no tests.
Every first-stage pool must be an arithmetic progression fixed before any answers are seen.
After receiving those answers, the scheme may query only O(k) individual positions in one final stage.
The question asks whether O(k log n) first-stage tests suffice for every hidden set, improving the bound reported in the 2009 source by one logarithmic factor.
The restriction models regularly spaced queries motivated by pattern matching, and unrestricted pooling results do not settle it.

definitions:
Write \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\). The input parameters \(n\) and \(k\) are known; only the subset \(S\) is hidden. The promise is an upper bound \(|S|\le k\), not knowledge of its exact size. In particular \(S=\varnothing\) is allowed. The elements have their fixed integer positions, and the arithmetic-progression constraint refers to these positions. There is no ability to permute the hidden input and then declare arbitrary pools to be progressions.

An admissible first-stage pool has the form
\[T=\{a,a+d,\ldots,a+(\ell-1)d\},\qquad a,d,\ell\in\mathbb N_{>0},\quad a+(\ell-1)d\le n.\]
Each pool may have its own start, step and length. Singletons are allowed. There is no wraparound modulo \(n\), no repeated item within a pool, and no requirement that the progression be extended to the ends of \([n]\). The answer is the noiseless bit \(b(T,S)=1\) if \(T\cap S\ne\varnothing\), and zero otherwise. It does not reveal the number or positions of the elements in the intersection.

For given \(n,k\), a scheme consists of a nonnegative integer \(m\), a list of admissible pools \(T_1,\ldots,T_m\), a selection function \(J\), and a final decoding function \(F\). The list depends only on \(n,k\); it is identical for every possible hidden set of the promised size. Write
\[y(S)=(b(T_1,S),\ldots,b(T_m,S))\in\{0,1\}^m.\]
The selection function takes any first-stage answer vector \(y\) to a set \(J(y)\subseteq[n]\) of indices with \(|J(y)|\le Dk\). Every selected index is queried separately, giving the function \(z_S:J(y(S))\to\{0,1\}\) defined by \(z_S(j)=1\) exactly when \(j\in S\). The final decoder knows the parameters, the entire first-stage design, \(y(S)\), the selected indices and their individual answers. Correctness means
\[\forall S\subseteq[n]\text{ with }|S|\le k:\quad F\bigl(y(S),z_S\bigr)=S.\]
The decoder may infer membership of unqueried indices from the complete transcript. It is not required to query every element that it finally reports. Queries in the second stage are individual membership tests only; no additional pooled tests or third stage are allowed. Unrealizable first-stage answer vectors can have arbitrary decoding behavior, subject to the same advertised second-stage query cap.

One test is one oracle answer, independent of the pool's cardinality. First-stage pools may be represented by their integer triples \((a,d,\ell)\), and individual indices and parameters in binary, but description length and computational time are not the costs asked about. No noise, random hidden-set distribution, random design, or probability of error is part of this formulation. This records the source's exact identification problem for an arbitrary set, as opposed to average-case recovery. An existence proof for the finite designs and functions suffices; a polynomial-time construction is not an extra requirement. Since all choices for fixed finite parameters can be enumerated and their correctness checked, this convention does not allow an undecidable query operation.

The quantifier order is \(\exists C,D>0\;\forall n,k\;\exists(T_1,\ldots,T_m,J,F)\;\forall S\), with the stated size restrictions. In particular a separate design tailored to the unknown \(S\) is inadmissible. The upper bound uses \(\log_2 n\), not \(\log_2(n/k)\). The source's \(O(k\log n)\) and \(O(k)\) mean absolute constant factors independent of both parameters. Using \(n\ge2\) avoids the irrelevant zero logarithm at one item.

A negative answer is the logical negation: for every proposed pair of constants \(C,D>0\), there are admissible \(n,k\) for which every scheme satisfying both test caps fails on some hidden set. It need not establish a particular alternative asymptotic lower-bound formula. A lower bound for a single family of progressions, a chosen decoder, or a nonadaptive one-stage scheme would not by itself disprove the target.
answer_criterion: Provide a complete Lean-checked proof or refutation of the existence of absolute constants and two-stage schemes with the stated bounds. A positive answer must prove the arithmetic-progression restriction, first-stage independence from answers, the \(O(k)\) cap on individual second-stage queries, and exact recovery for every hidden set of size at most \(k\), uniformly over the full parameter domain. A negative answer must rule out all allowed designs and decoders with every proposed pair of constant factors. Results allowing arbitrary first-stage pools, more rounds, non-individual second-stage tests, or error on some hidden sets do not settle this proposition. This is an asymptotic existence question, so additive numerical tolerance is inapplicable.

source_formulation.text: Porat asks whether two-stage exact group testing can use \(O(k\log n)\) first-stage pools when each pool is an arithmetic progression. Only \(O(k)\) individually chosen membership tests are allowed in the second stage. The listed benchmark for the progression-restricted first stage is \(O(k\log^2 n)\).
source_formulation.caption: Editorial paraphrase of Sublinear.info Problem 33; the progression restriction and both stages are retained

context_blocks.text: The hidden set represents a sparse collection of relevant positions. A pooled answer identifies whether an entire regular selection of positions contains any relevant element, so many positions can be checked with one bit of feedback.

The central restriction concerns which collections can be tested together. An arithmetic progression has a fixed spacing, as occurs when inspecting regularly sampled positions in pattern-matching applications. A result for arbitrary subsets does not automatically provide such regularly spaced pools.

The source permits one round of adaptation: pooled answers can determine which individual positions will be checked next. Its question asks whether this limited feedback compensates for the restriction on first-stage pools.

The 2009 question reports \(O(k\log^2 n)\) first-stage tests under the arithmetic-progression restriction and asks to remove one logarithmic factor. This is a dated benchmark reported by the problem proposer, not a newly verified 2026 optimality claim.

The unrestricted two-stage setting has order-optimal test-count results in the cited 2005 paper. Its publisher abstract confirms that the main theorem concerns unrestricted intersection queries, with other variants treated separately. This comparison explains why the geometry of the permitted pools is the substantive issue here.

The inherited card contained only the topic name. The full problem page supplies the two stages, the progression restriction and the desired bound. This review preserves that target and makes the worst-case, zero-error and test-count-only conventions explicit. It does not add efficient construction or a distributional recovery promise.
